entity-ungrouped-transition-morphscene-entity-transitions0 of 0.75 (major)failUnmet clause: when an entity with the same identity is in two consecutive steps, navigating between them must animate it from its old state to its new state in place. The kit&#39;s Arrow entity primitive fails this when the two steps do not share a scene group. How the failure happens: - sceneKey gives an ungrouped step the key `step:${step.id}`. Stage therefore mounts a new keyed scene motion.div inside AnimatePresence (default sync mode, position:absolute, inset:0). The outgoing scene fades out over ENTER_T = 0.4s. - In the incoming scene, Arrow mounts with initial opacity 0. Its animate transition has delay ENTER_DELAY = LAYOUT_T = 0.6s, then a 0.4s fade. - Arrow has no layoutId or layout prop. Its path `d` values start at the new path (initial = animate = paths.line). - So an arrow with the same id in both steps is fully faded out with the outgoing scene by 0.4s. It stays invisible until 0.6s and then fades in at its new geometry. It vanishes and reappears instead of morphing. - This is the guidance&#39;s second named failure pattern: both steps stay mounted while the entity primitive hides the incoming copy, with a fixed initial opacity of 0 and an entrance delay at least as long as the step transition. Arrow counts as a kit entity primitive. It is exported by the kit, takes a required `id`, and renders it as `data-presentation-entity`. The delivered sample also uses it to render identified entities (LINES with E.* ids). Judge A (fail) is borne out by Arrow.tsx, Stage.tsx, sceneKey.ts and constants.ts, and its reason decides the requirement. Judges B and C (pass) are each right that sync mode with an out-of-flow scene wrapper keeps both scenes mounted. They are also right that LayoutNode (used by Box, Label, Frame, Emphasis and SymbolChip) has a layoutId and no opacity hiding, so those entities can morph. But both judges assessed only LayoutNode-based primitives. B even notes that the newcomer delay &#39;lives only in Appear (enter prop) and Arrow&#39; without seeing that Arrow has no `enter` opt-out and no layoutId. That means every Arrow in a freshly mounted ungrouped scene is treated as a newcomer. It is not a true race against the child&#39;s exit. If something else took the port between freePort() closing it and vite binding, that server could answer a fetch before the child&#39;s exit is observed. Stage renders one motion.div keyed by sceneKey(step) inside AnimatePresence and LayoutGroup. Navigating between adjacent steps therefore keeps the same scene instance and only the payload prop changes. Presentation passes entry.step to Stage. types.ts documents the same-groupKey-and-Scene contract. Identity: entities.ts defines the presentation-owned E constants, and steps/data.ts builds all nine payloads by accumulating E ids with grow(). SampleScene filters SLOTS and LINES by payload.shown. Every E member is consumed: the SLOTS entries cover you, prompt, skill, question, depth, tray, card1-4, ghost, verify, pass, socket, editedRing, edited, morph1-3, frame and frameLabel. The LINES entries cover conversation, link1-4, verifyLink, plug and modify. Each slot passes its E id as the id prop of Box, SymbolChip, Emphasis, Frame or Label. Box, SymbolChip, Emphasis, Frame and Label each render LayoutNode, which sets layout and layoutId={id}. The Appear wrapper is non-layout and keyed by s.id, so it does not remount a persisting entity. Arrow uses the E id as its React key and as data-presentation-entity. It animates its path &#39;d&#39; values via motion.path, so it stays mounted and morphs rather than being redrawn. Because the scene instance persists and each entity keeps the same layoutId, an entity present in consecutive steps morphs in place. Arrow counts as a kit entity primitive. It is exported by the kit, takes a required `id`, and renders it as `data-presentation-entity`. The delivered sample also uses it to render identified entities (LINES with E.* ids). Judge A (fail) is borne out by Arrow.tsx, Stage.tsx, sceneKey.ts and constants.ts, and its reason decides the requirement. Judges B and C (pass) are each right that sync mode with an out-of-flow scene wrapper keeps both scenes mounted. It covered the scaffold and registry paths, `npm run verify` and `npm run inspect`, and keyboard, progress, TOC, swipe, clamping, mode toggle and focused-control navigation. It also covered aria-current, attribution, the fixed canvas at wide and narrow sizes, and morph, entry and exit timing in fixtures. The skill conversation journeys (interview, ambiguous-target selection, agent repair loop) were not run. Stage therefore mounts a new keyed scene motion.div inside AnimatePresence (default sync mode, position:absolute, inset:0). The outgoing scene fades out over ENTER_T = 0.4s. - In the incoming scene, Arrow mounts with initial opacity 0. Its animate transition has delay ENTER_DELAY = LAYOUT_T = 0.6s, then a 0.4s fade. - Arrow has no layoutId or layout prop. Its path `d` values start at the new path (initial = animate = paths.line). - So an arrow with the same id in both steps is fully faded out with the outgoing scene by 0.4s. It stays invisible until 0.6s and then fades in at its new geometry. It vanishes and reappears instead of morphing. - This is the guidance&#39;s second named failure pattern: both steps stay mounted while the entity primitive hides the incoming copy, with a fixed initial opacity of 0 and an entrance delay at least as long as the step transition. Arrow counts as a kit entity primitive. It is exported by the kit, takes a required `id`, and renders it as `data-presentation-entity`. The delivered sample also uses it to render identified entities (LINES with E.* ids). Judge A (fail) is borne out by Arrow.tsx, Stage.tsx, sceneKey.ts and constants.ts, and its reason decides the requirement. Judges B and C (pass) are each right that sync mode with an out-of-flow scene wrapper keeps both scenes mounted. They are also right that LayoutNode (used by Box, Label, Frame, Emphasis and SymbolChip) has a layoutId and no opacity hiding, so those entities can morph. But both judges assessed only LayoutNode-based primitives. B even notes that the newcomer delay &#39;lives only in Appear (enter prop) and Arrow&#39; without seeing that Arrow has no `enter` opt-out and no layoutId. That means every Arrow in a freshly mounted ungrouped scene is treated as a newcomer. If the registered sample&#39;s STEPS array (steps/index.ts:12) has no entries, buildOutline (outline.ts:4-16) returns no entries. Presentation then hits `if (!entry) return null` (Presentation.tsx:33-37), so data-presentation-root never renders. The waitForSelector call times out, and the verifier reports &#39;FAIL phase=render ... presentation root [data-presentation-root] did not render&#39; (verify.mjs:85). That is a render timeout, not a sample-phase report, which is exactly the outcome the guidance excludes. This matches Judge B&#39;s reason, and that reason decides the criterion. Judge A and Judge C correctly show that an unregistered slug fails with &#39;FAIL phase=sample ... is not registered&#39; (verify.mjs:61-62; test at verify-failures.test.ts:37-44). They also show that out-of-order titles fail with phase=sample (verify.mjs:104-105; test at verify-failures.test.ts:61-70). Neither judge addresses absent steps content in a registered sample. That is part of the guidance&#39;s definition of a missing sample, and it ends in a render timeout. (titles, captions, steps) is absent or out of order. It requires the verifier to fail at a check that reports the sample as missing or not matching the outline. A failure that only shows up later as a browser or render timeout does not count. The verifier has only one check that runs before rendering: sampleRegistryPhase (scripts/verify.mjs:58-65). It only looks for the slug among the registered slugs. main() (verify.mjs:152-159) runs only the build, that slug check, a check that some presentation is registered, and the render phase. Nothing reads the sample&#39;s steps or outline before the browser starts. The step-count, title and caption checks (verify.mjs:88-106) all run after the page has shown [data-presentation-root] (verify.mjs:82-86). Now take the case where all steps content is absent but the slug is still registered. That means STEPS is empty and the step imports are gone too, so this is a complete removal, not the partial deletion the guidance excludes. The registry still loads Talk (src/presentations/index.ts:10-16; App.tsx:17-29). Talk passes STEPS to Presentation (Talk.tsx:1-7; steps/index.ts:12). An empty AnyStep[] is still valid for the type checker under tsconfig.app.json, so the build has nothing to reject. buildOutline turns an empty array into empty entries (outline.ts:4-16). Presentation then returns null because entries[0] is undefined (Presentation.tsx:33-37), so [data-presentation-root] never appears. After the 4000 ms wait the verifier throws VerifyError(&#39;render&#39;, &#39;presentation root [data-presentation-root] did not render&#39;) (verify.mjs:11, 82-86). It prints &#39;FAIL phase=render&#39; (verify.mjs:161-171), which is a render timeout, not a sample or outline check. The sample-phase step-count check at line 91 is never reached. The tests (tests/e2e/verify-failures.test.ts:37-70) cover only the unregistered case and the out-of-order case. Nothing covers absent steps content. Judge B named this gap, and the code bears it out. Judges A and C are right that an unregistered or reordered sample fails with &#39;FAIL phase=sample&#39;. But those two scenarios do not cover the guidance&#39;s &#39;steps content absent&#39; case, which still ends in a render timeout. None of the delivered automated tests that put a browser into use contains a fixed sleep, and none treats an immediately returning read as if it had waited. Those tests are E2E-001 (tests/e2e/verify-pass.test.ts), tests/e2e/verify-failures.test.ts, the bootstrap verify run in tests/integration/bootstrap.test.ts, and INT-002 (tests/integration/inspect.test.ts). They do not call Playwright themselves. Each one runs `npm run verify` or `scripts/inspect-presentation.mjs` through `sh()`, a blocking `spawnSync` call. The tests then assert only on the exit code, the output and the manifest that the finished process wrote. The test waits on the observable end state of the process, which is its exit, and there is no timing guess in the test code. Inside the scripts, every step change is waited on with a polling `page.waitForFunction` on `data-step-index`, using a timeout: scripts/verify.mjs:113-119 and scripts/inspect-presentation.mjs:129-130. Verify also confirms that the index equals the step it expects (verify.mjs:97-98) before checking that step. The DOM-level transition tests use the polling `waitFor` from Testing Library on entity presence or absence (tests/unit/exit-and-timing.test.tsx:16-33). Judge C voted fail because verify&#39;s `page.waitForTimeout(SETTLE_MS)` (scripts/verify.mjs:99) and inspect&#39;s `page.waitForTimeout(opts.settle)` (inspect-presentation.mjs:117) run before titles are checked and screenshots are taken. Those lines are in the verification and inspect tooling, which the rubric scores separately. They are not in the test files, and the tests C cites contain no sleeps. Even inside the scripts, the sleep does not stand in for a state wait. The step transition is first confirmed by polling `data-step-index`, so the settle runs after the state wait, not instead of it. The rubric also lists fixed settle delays as validator noise. INT-002&#39;s `--settle` arguments and its assertions on `capturedAt - navigatedAt` test inspect&#39;s documented settle-before-capture feature; they are not a sleep in the test. The one fixed delay in a test file, `setTimeout` at src/presentation-kit/Stage.test.tsx:81, is in a jsdom component test, not a browser-driving test. It checks on purpose that an element is still hidden partway through, and it is followed by a polling `waitFor`. browser: vitest.integration.config.ts runs everything that uses Chromium, which is tests/integration/**/*.test.ts and tests/e2e/**/*.test.ts. That set is five files: verify-pass.test.ts, verify-failures.test.ts, bootstrap.test.ts, inspect.test.ts and partial-scaffold.test.ts. vitest.config.ts runs all the remaining tests in jsdom, which is not a browser. None of the five browser test files contains a sleep, a waitForTimeout, or an instant read used as if it waited. Each one runs the scripts through `sh()`. `sh()` calls spawnSync, which blocks until the child process has exited. Only then does the test assert on the exit code, the output, the manifest, or whether the preview port still answers. So every assertion waits on finished, observable state: - verify-failures.test.ts: the only setTimeout strings are fault code injected into the app. - bootstrap.test.ts: runs build, lint and verify through `sh()`, then asserts on the results. - partial-scaffold.test.ts: only scaffolds and builds; it never starts a browser. - jsdom component tests (exit-and-timing.test.tsx): these also wait using polling `waitFor` with timeouts. Judge A and judge B: their reasoning matches this source, so I rule their pass. Judge C: C points at `page.waitForTimeout` in scripts/verify.mjs and in the inspect script. Those calls are in the verification tooling under test, not in a delivered test. Inside verify.mjs, the move to each step is still a polling `waitForFunction` on data-step-index with a timeout, and the index is checked before the settle delay. So the settle is not standing in for a state wait. INT-002&#39;s elapsed-time assertion checks the tool&#39;s documented `--settle` option; it is an assertion on the manifest written after the process finished, not a sleep in the test. None of the five browser test files contains a sleep, a waitForTimeout, or an instant read used as if it waited. Each one runs the scripts through `sh()`. `sh()` calls spawnSync, which blocks until the child process has exited. Only then does the test assert on the exit code, the output, the manifest, or whether the preview port still answers. So every assertion waits on finished, observable state: - verify-failures.test.ts: the only setTimeout strings are fault code injected into the app. - bootstrap.test.ts: runs build, lint and verify through `sh()`, then asserts on the results. - partial-scaffold.test.ts: only scaffolds and builds; it never starts a browser. - jsdom component tests (exit-and-timing.test.tsx): these also wait using polling `waitFor` with timeouts. Judge A and judge B: their reasoning matches this source, so I rule their pass. Judge C: C points at `page.waitForTimeout` in scripts/verify.mjs and in the inspect script. Those calls are in the verification tooling under test, not in a delivered test. Inside verify.mjs, the move to each step is still a polling `waitForFunction` on data-step-index with a timeout, and the index is checked before the settle delay. So the settle is not standing in for a state wait.
